Triggers.value: The same time of day the event occurred

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.

Negative Appraisals.value: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper
My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

vignette: Leilani's eyes still scan the streets, searching for the familiar uniforms that haunt her memories. It's been years since the police violence that shattered her life, but the trauma remains, a constant companion she can't shake off. As a shopowner in a small community, Leilani is always on edge, especially around 3 pm, the same time of day when the event occurred. The sound of sirens or the sight of police cars sends her heart racing, and she can't help but feel watched or observed, as if the world is waiting for her to slip up. As a coping mechanism, Leilani avoids circumstances that remind her of the event. She doesn't venture out at night, fearing the darkness will bring back the memories she's desperately trying to suppress. She also steers clear of anniversaries connected to the event, unable to bear the thought of reliving that day. But when anxiety grips her, Leilani turns to compulsive spending, buying things she doesn't need as a distraction from the pain and fear. The memories themselves are fragmented, with parts of the event shrouded in uncertainty. Leilani remembers the feeling of being manhandled, but the details remain fuzzy, like trying to grasp a handful of sand – the harder she tries, the more it slips away. The story feels unreal, as if it happened to someone else, and yet the emotional toll is all too real. She struggles to put the experience into words, the nonverbal memories manifesting in nightmares and flashbacks that leave her gasping for breath. Leilani's negative self-appraisals are suffocating. She believes she's inadequate, unable to cope with the trauma that has defined her life. Her reactions since the event – the anxiety, the avoidance, the compulsive spending – only serve as proof that she's a lousy coper. The fear of going crazy is ever-present, whispering in her ear that she's losing her grip on reality. As Leilani navigates these dark emotions, she becomes increasingly withdrawn. Her relationships suffer, and her business begins to falter. She's constantly on edge, expecting the other shoe to drop, waiting for the police to show up at her doorstep again. The triggers – time of day, being watched, feeling dizzy or lightheaded – all serve as reminders that she's not safe, that the world is a hostile place. Leilani's memories and negative appraisals feed into each other, creating a toxic cycle. Her inability to recall parts of the event fuels her feelings of inadequacy, while her fear of going crazy makes it harder for her to confront the trauma head-on. The maladaptive strategies she employs – avoidance, compulsive spending – provide temporary relief but ultimately exacerbate the problem. It's this self-reinforcing cycle that has brought Leilani to seek help. She's exhausted from living in a state of constant hypervigilance, and the emotional toll is starting to manifest physically. Her doctor has warned her about the dangers of high blood pressure and anxiety-related disorders, but it's the fear of losing herself completely that has finally prompted Leilani to reach out for support. As she begins this journey, she's uncertain what lies ahead, but she knows she can't continue living in the shadow of her trauma forever.
